title: Grade 7 French — Tue, May 19
description: Le verbe avoir (The verb to have) — Day 2 of 5: Conjugation and key uses
subject: french

questions.question: What is 'I have' in French?
questions.explanation: 'J'ai' = I have. Note: 'je' + 'ai' contract to 'j'ai' before a vowel. Avoir: j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont.

questions.question: Complete: 'Tu ___ un chien?' (avoir)
questions.explanation: 'Tu as un chien?' = Do you have a dog? 'As' is the 'tu' form of avoir.

questions.question: What is the 'ils' form of avoir?
questions.explanation: 'Ils ont' = they have. Full avoir: j'ai / tu as / il-elle a / nous avons / vous avez / ils-elles ont.

questions.question: In French, 'avoir' is used for age. How do you say 'She is 13 years old'?
questions.explanation: 'Elle a treize ans' = She is 13 (literally 'she has 13 years'). French uses 'avoir' for age, unlike English which uses 'to be'.

questions.question: Avoir is also used for physical sensations. 'J'ai faim.' means:
questions.explanation: 'J'ai faim' = I am hungry (literally 'I have hunger'). French uses 'avoir' for: faim(hungry), soif(thirsty), chaud(hot), froid(cold), peur(afraid), raison(right), tort(wrong), sommeil(sleepy).

questions.question: How do you say 'We have two cats'?
questions.explanation: 'Nous avons deux chats' = We have two cats. 'Avons' is the 'nous' form of avoir.

questions.question: What does 'Il a l'air fatigué.' mean?
options: He looks tired (avoir l'air = to look/seem)
questions.explanation: 'Avoir l'air + adjective' = to look/seem. 'Il a l'air fatigué' = He looks/seems tired. This idiom always uses avoir, not être.

questions.question: How do you say 'She is afraid of spiders'?
questions.explanation: 'Avoir peur de' = to be afraid of. 'Elle a peur des araignées' = She is afraid of spiders. Another key 'avoir' expression.

questions.question: Translate: 'You (formal) have a beautiful house.'
questions.explanation: 'Vous avez une belle maison' = You have a beautiful house. 'Belle' (f) agrees with 'maison' (f). 'Avez' = vous form.

questions.question: When is 'avoir' used as an AUXILIARY verb?
options: Never — only être is used as auxiliary
For forming passé composé of most verbs (j'ai mangé, tu as fini...)
questions.explanation: Avoir is the auxiliary (helping verb) for forming passé composé of MOST French verbs: j'ai mangé (I ate), tu as fini (you finished). Exceptions use être.

questions.question: 'Nous avons chaud.' — What does this mean?
options: We are warm / we feel hot.
questions.explanation: 'Avoir chaud' = to be/feel warm. Like 'avoir faim', French uses 'avoir' for physical states: chaud(warm), froid(cold). 'Nous avons chaud' = We feel hot.

questions.question: What is the negative of 'J'ai un frère'?
options: Je ne pas ai un frère.
questions.explanation: 'Je n'ai pas de frère' = I don't have a brother. After negation with 'avoir', the indefinite article (un/une/des) changes to 'de/d'': 'J'ai un frère' → 'Je n'ai pas de frère'.

questions.question: 'Vous avez raison.' What does this mean?
options: You have a reason to be angry.
questions.explanation: 'Avoir raison' = to be right. 'Avoir tort' = to be wrong. These are fixed expressions using avoir.

questions.question: How old is someone who says 'J'ai quinze ans'?
questions.explanation: 'Quinze' = 15. 'J'ai quinze ans' = I am 15 years old. 'Ans' = years.

questions.question: Give all 6 forms of avoir:
questions.explanation: Avoir: j'ai / tu as / il-elle a / nous avons / vous avez / ils-elles ont. Together with être, these are the two most essential French verbs.
